claim: Phytate is the major form of phosphorus in plant seeds, accounting for up to 80% of total phosphorous.
source: Phytate (Myo-inositol hexaphosphate) is the main phosphorus storage system in plant seeds such as those of cereal grains, nuts, oilseeds, and legumes (Raboy, 2000; Reddy et al., 1982), accounting for up to 80% of total phosphorous.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Raboy, 2000; Reddy et al., 1982) establishing this as known scientific knowledge.

claim: Phytate tightly binds to essential minerals such as Ca2+, Mg2+, Fe2+, and Zn2+ to form mineral-phytate salts because of its six phosphate groups.
source: Phytate tightly binds to essential minerals such as Ca2+, Mg2+, Fe2+, and Zn2+ to form mineral-phytate salts because of its six phosphate groups (Kim et al., 2010; Oh et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Kim et al., 2010; Oh et al., 2006) and represents established knowledge about phytate chemistry.

claim: Mineral-phytate salts are known to be indigestible by monogastric animals and humans, which lack the digestive enzyme phytase.
source: These mineral-phytate salts are known to be indigestible by monogastric animals and humans, which lack the digestive enzyme phytase that releases phosphate from mineral-phytate salts (Reddy and Sathe, 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior research (Reddy and Sathe, 2002) and represents the prevailing hypothesis in the field.

claim: The prevailing hypothesis argues that phytate-derived phosphorus is indigestible, not absorbed in the intestine, and is excreted in the feces.
source: The prevailing hypothesis argues that phytate-derived phosphorus is indigestible, not absorbed in the intestine, and is excreted in the feces (Golovan et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior research (Golovan et al., 2001) and describes the existing scientific consensus.

claim: Excessive intake of phytate along with a low-Ca2+ diet fed to rats contributed to the development of crystal nephropathies, renal phosphate wasting, and bone loss.
source: Here, we show that excessive intake of phytate along with a low-Ca2+ diet fed to rats contributed to the development of crystal nephropathies, renal phosphate wasting, and bone loss through tubular dysfunction secondary to dysregulation of intestinal calcium and phosphate absorption.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data from rat feeding studies described throughout the manuscript.

claim: Ca2+ supplementation alleviated the detrimental effects of excess dietary phytate on bone and kidney through excretion of undigested Ca2+-phytate.
source: Moreover, Ca2+ supplementation alleviated the detrimental effects of excess dietary phytate on bone and kidney through excretion of undigested Ca2+-phytate, which prevented a vicious cycle of intestinal phosphate overload and renal phosphate wasting while improving intestinal Ca2+ bioavailability.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data comparing high-phytate diets with different calcium levels.

claim: Phytate is digestible without a high-Ca2+ diet.
source: Thus, we demonstrate that phytate is digestible without a high-Ca2+ diet and is a risk factor for phosphate overloading and for the development of crystal nephropathies and bone disease.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study supported by fecal analysis data showing phytate hydrolysis in low-calcium conditions.

claim: Rats fed higher levels of phytate (3% and 5%) exhibited decreased growth rates compared with controls.
source: Rats that were fed higher levels of phytate (3% and 5%) exhibited decreased growth rates and reduced fat-free lean mass and whole-body fat compared with those of the control, despite similar daily food intake (Figure 1C–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by body weight measurements shown in Figure 1C-F and described in the text.

claim: Rats fed higher levels of phytate (3% and 5%) exhibited reduced fat-free lean mass and whole-body fat compared with controls, despite similar daily food intake.
source: Rats that were fed higher levels of phytate (3% and 5%) exhibited decreased growth rates and reduced fat-free lean mass and whole-body fat compared with those of the control, despite similar daily food intake (Figure 1C–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by body composition measurements shown in Figure 1E-F and described in the text.

claim: Dietary phytate led to the inhibition of intestinal absorption of essential minerals such as Ca2+, Mg2+, and Fe2+ in a concentration-dependent manner.
source: We found that dietary phytate led to the inhibition of intestinal absorption of essential minerals such as Ca2+, Mg2+, and Fe2+ in a concentration-dependent manner (Figure 1G–H, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by ICP-MS analysis of fecal minerals shown in Figure 1G-H and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: High-phytate-fed rats developed hypophosphatemia.
source: High-phytate-fed rats developed hypophosphatemia (Figure 1J) and hypomagnesemia (Figure 1k).
evidence: The claim is supported by serum phosphate measurements shown in Figure 1J.

claim: High-phytate-fed rats developed hypomagnesemia.
source: High-phytate-fed rats developed hypophosphatemia (Figure 1J) and hypomagnesemia (Figure 1k).
evidence: The claim is supported by serum magnesium measurements shown in Figure 1K.

claim: Parathyroid hormone (PTH) levels markedly increased (5.4–11.7-fold) in the high-phytate groups by week 5.
source: Parathyroid hormone (PTH) levels markedly increased (5.4–11.7-fold) in the high-phytate groups by week 5 (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) and remained elevated (2.8–6.4-fold) to week 12 (Figure 1L) in all phytate-fed rats because of sustained inhibition of intestinal Ca2+ absorption.
evidence: The claim is supported by PTH measurements shown in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: PTH levels remained elevated (2.8–6.4-fold) to week 12 in all phytate-fed rats.
source: Parathyroid hormone (PTH) levels markedly increased (5.4–11.7-fold) in the high-phytate groups by week 5 (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) and remained elevated (2.8–6.4-fold) to week 12 (Figure 1L) in all phytate-fed rats because of sustained inhibition of intestinal Ca2+ absorption.
evidence: The claim is supported by PTH measurements shown in Figure 1L.

claim: Rats exhibited a large increase in the BUN/Cr ratio in all phytate groups.
source: Rats exhibited a large increase in the BUN/Cr ratio in all phytate groups (Figure 1M, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by BUN/Cr ratio measurements shown in Figure 1M and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Rats fed 5% phytate had multiple renal cysts at the corticomedullary junction.
source: MRI analysis revealed that rats fed 5% phytate had multiple renal cysts at the corticomedullary junction (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by MRI images shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The kidneys of rats fed 5% phytate exhibited pronounced renomegaly with pitted, irregular, and granular cortices and medullar morphology.
source: The kidneys of these rats exhibited pronounced renomegaly with pitted, irregular, and granular cortices and medullar morphology (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by gross morphological observations shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B-C.

claim: The severity of renal injury was greatest in female rats fed 3% or 5% phytate and in male rats fed 5% phytate.
source: The severity of renal injury was greatest in female rats fed 3% or 5% phytate and in male rats fed 5% phytate, whereas control rats lacked significant pathological changes.
evidence: The claim is supported by histopathological scoring of kidney sections described in the text.

claim: Phytate-fed rats exhibited marked decreases in the rates of bone accrual along with decreased bone mineral density (BMD) in a concentration-dependent manner.
source: Phytate-fed rats exhibited marked decreases in the rates of bone accrual along with decreased bone mineral density (BMD) in a concentration-dependent manner when compared with controls (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by pDEXA measurements shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Phytate-fed rats exhibited significantly decreased trabecular bone volume (BV/TV), trabecular bone surface (BS/TV), trabecular number (Tb.N), and significantly increased trabecular space (Tb.Sp) compared with controls.
source: Further, phytate-fed rats exhibited significantly decreased trabecular bone volume (BV/TV), trabecular bone surface (BS/TV), trabecular number (Tb.N), and significantly increased trabecular space (Tb.Sp) compared with controls (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by μ-CT analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Phytate-fed rats had markedly reduced cortical bone area (Tt.Ar) and increased cortical area fractions (Ct.Ar/Tt.Ar).
source: Consistent with the trabecular bone phenotypes, phytate-fed rats had markedly reduced cortical bone area (Tt.Ar) and increased cortical area fractions (Ct.Ar/Tt.Ar) (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by μ-CT analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Serum levels of receptor activator of nuclear factor kappa-B ligand (RANKL) were markedly increased in high-phytate-fed rats compared with controls.
source: Serum levels of receptor activator of nuclear factor kappa-B ligand (RANKL), a key component of osteoclastogenesis (Kong et al., 1999), were markedly increased in high-phytate-fed rats compared with controls (Figure 3F).
evidence: The claim is supported by ELISA measurements shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The levels of osteoprotegerin (OPG) were significantly reduced in phytate-fed rats.
source: The levels of osteoprotegerin (OPG), a RANKL decoy receptor that inhibits osteoclast differentiation and activation (Lacey et al., 1998), were significantly reduced (Figure 3G), and the sRANKL/OPG ratio was significantly increased in phytate-fed rats (Figure 3H).
evidence: The claim is supported by ELISA measurements shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The sRANKL/OPG ratio was significantly increased in phytate-fed rats.
source: The levels of osteoprotegerin (OPG), a RANKL decoy receptor that inhibits osteoclast differentiation and activation (Lacey et al., 1998), were significantly reduced (Figure 3G), and the sRANKL/OPG ratio was significantly increased in phytate-fed rats (Figure 3H).
evidence: The claim is supported by calculated ratios from ELISA measurements shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Consumption of the high-phytate diet resulted in increased TRAP+ multinucleated cells.
source: Analysis of bone sections stained for tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase (TRAP) revealed that consumption of the high-phytate diet resulted in increased TRAP+ multinucleated cells (Figure 3I).
evidence: The claim is supported by TRAP staining shown in Figure 3I.

claim: Bone marrow-derived stromal cell cultures exhibited a significant concentration-dependent increase in the number of giant TRAP+ multinucleated osteoclasts.
source: Further, bone marrow-derived stromal cell cultures exhibited a significant concentration-dependent increase in the number of giant TRAP+ multinucleated osteoclasts (Figure 3J).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro osteoclast differentiation assays shown in Figure 3J.

claim: High dietary phytate intake was associated with slightly decreased serum phosphate levels in humans.
source: Serum levels of Ca2+, magnesium, and phosphate remained within the normal range for all three diets, although high dietary phytate intake was associated with slightly decreased serum phosphate levels (Figure 4B–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by serum measurements from the human pilot study shown in Figure 4B-C.

claim: Urinary pH levels decreased in a dose-dependent manner as the intake of phytate increased in humans.
source: Urinary pH levels decreased in a dose-dependent manner as the intake of phytate increased (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by urine pH measurements from the human pilot study shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Higher dietary phytate intake resulted in a marked decrease in the 24 hr urinary Ca2+ creatinine clearance rate in humans.
source: Higher dietary phytate intake resulted in a marked decrease in the 24 hr urinary Ca2+ creatinine clearance rate (Figure 4E), whereas the 24 hr urinary phosphate creatinine clearance rate was only slightly increased (Figure 4F).
evidence: The claim is supported by 24-hour urine measurements from the human pilot study shown in Figure 4E.

claim: High dietary phytate increases the renal tubular Ca2+ reabsorption rate in humans.
source: These findings are consistent with the results of the tubular reabsorption rate, where high dietary phytate increases the renal tubular Ca2+ reabsorption rate (Figure 4G) but decreases the renal tubular phosphate reabsorption rate (Figure 4H).
evidence: The claim is supported by calculated tubular reabsorption rates from the human pilot study shown in Figure 4G.

claim: High dietary phytate decreases the renal tubular phosphate reabsorption rate in humans.
source: These findings are consistent with the results of the tubular reabsorption rate, where high dietary phytate increases the renal tubular Ca2+ reabsorption rate (Figure 4G) but decreases the renal tubular phosphate reabsorption rate (Figure 4H).
evidence: The claim is supported by calculated tubular reabsorption rates from the human pilot study shown in Figure 4H.

claim: High dietary phytate intake increases PTH levels in humans.
source: These metabolic characteristics are probably secondary to the increased levels of PTH that occur in response to high levels of dietary phytate intake (Figure 4I).
evidence: The claim is supported by PTH measurements from the human pilot study shown in Figure 4I.

claim: High dietary phytate decreased the serum levels of FGF23 in humans.
source: Further, high dietary phytate decreased the serum levels of FGF23 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by FGF23 measurements from the human pilot study shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Rats fed the HP-HCa2+ diet completely normalized their serum levels of phosphate and BUN compared with rats fed the HP-LCa2+ diet.
source: Moreover, rats fed the HP-HCa2+ diet completely normalized their serum levels of phosphate and BUN, as well as the BUN/Cr ratio compared with rats fed the HP-LCa2+ diet (Figure 5B–C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1E), indicating that supplementation with high Ca2+ ameliorated hypophosphatemia and azotemia.
evidence: The claim is supported by serum biochemistry measurements shown in Figure 5B-C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Rats fed the HP-LCa2+ diet had markedly decreased urine pH compared with controls.
source: Rats fed the HP-LCa2+ diet had markedly decreased urine pH (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F) without significant differences in urine volume (Figure 5—figure supplement 1G), marked decreases in the 24 hr urinary Ca2+/Cr ratio (Figure 5D), and a marked increase in the 24 hr urinary Pi/Cr ratio (Figure 5E) compared with controls.
evidence: The claim is supported by urine pH measurements shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Rats fed the HP-LCa2+ diet had marked decreases in the 24 hr urinary Ca2+/Cr ratio compared with controls.
source: Rats fed the HP-LCa2+ diet had markedly decreased urine pH (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F) without significant differences in urine volume (Figure 5—figure supplement 1G), marked decreases in the 24 hr urinary Ca2+/Cr ratio (Figure 5D), and a marked increase in the 24 hr urinary Pi/Cr ratio (Figure 5E) compared with controls.
evidence: The claim is supported by 24-hour urine measurements shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Rats fed the HP-LCa2+ diet had a marked increase in the 24 hr urinary Pi/Cr ratio compared with controls.
source: Rats fed the HP-LCa2+ diet had markedly decreased urine pH (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F) without significant differences in urine volume (Figure 5—figure supplement 1G), marked decreases in the 24 hr urinary Ca2+/Cr ratio (Figure 5D), and a marked increase in the 24 hr urinary Pi/Cr ratio (Figure 5E) compared with controls.
evidence: The claim is supported by 24-hour urine measurements shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Rats fed the HP-LCa2+ diet had markedly higher renal tubular reabsorption of Ca2+ (TmCa2+/GFR) compared with controls.
source: Further, rats fed the HP-LCa2+ diet had markedly higher renal tubular reabsorption of Ca2+ (TmCa2+/GFR), with lower renal tubular reabsorption of phosphate (TmP/GFR) compared with controls (Figure 5F–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by calculated tubular reabsorption rates shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Rats fed the HP-LCa2+ diet had lower renal tubular reabsorption of phosphate (TmP/GFR) compared with controls.
source: Further, rats fed the HP-LCa2+ diet had markedly higher renal tubular reabsorption of Ca2+ (TmCa2+/GFR), with lower renal tubular reabsorption of phosphate (TmP/GFR) compared with controls (Figure 5F–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by calculated tubular reabsorption rates shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Rats fed the HP-HCa2+ diet excreted an approximately three-fold higher level of fecal phytate compared with rats fed the HP-LCa2+ diet.
source: High-performance ion chromatographic (HPIC) analysis of feces demonstrated that rats fed the HP-HCa2+ diet excreted an approximately three-fold higher level of fecal phytate compared with rats fed the HP-LCa2+ diet (Figure 5H–I).
evidence: The claim is supported by HPIC analysis of fecal samples shown in Figure 5H-I.

claim: Rats fed the HP-HCa2+ diet exhibited an approximately 3.8-fold greater increase in Ca2+ and phosphate excretion compared with rats fed the HP-LCa2+ diet.
source: ICP-MS analysis, performed after acid hydrolysis of fecal phytate to generate phosphate, further confirmed that rats fed the HP-HCa2+ diet exhibited an approximately 3.8-fold greater increase in Ca2+ and phosphate excretion compared with rats fed the HP-LCa2+ diet (Figure 5J–K), confirming findings of increased fecal excretion of undigested Ca2+-phytate in rats fed the HP-HCa2+ diet.
evidence: The claim is supported by ICP-MS analysis of fecal samples shown in Figure 5J-K.

claim: Rats fed the HP-LCa2+ diet hydrolyzed and absorbed >68–74% of the phosphate in the intestine.
source: Conversely, rats fed the HP-LCa2+ diet hydrolyzed and absorbed >68–74% of the phosphate in the intestine (Figure 5H–K) with a concomitant increase in urinary phosphate excretion, thus developing renal phosphate wasting (Figure 5E–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by fecal phytate analysis shown in Figure 5H-K.

claim: Rats fed the HP-LCa2+ diet had significantly higher levels of Firmicutes, Bacteroidetes, and β-Proteobacteria compared to controls.
source: Phylum-level analysis indicated that rats fed the HP-LCa2+ diet had significantly higher levels of Firmicutes, Bacteroidetes, and β-Proteobacteria, but had markedly lower levels of Actinobacteria compared to controls (Figure 5—figure supplement 2E–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative real-time PCR analysis of fecal microbiota shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2E-H.

claim: Rats fed the HP-LCa2+ diet had markedly lower levels of Actinobacteria compared to controls.
source: Phylum-level analysis indicated that rats fed the HP-LCa2+ diet had significantly higher levels of Firmicutes, Bacteroidetes, and β-Proteobacteria, but had markedly lower levels of Actinobacteria compared to controls (Figure 5—figure supplement 2E–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative real-time PCR analysis of fecal microbiota shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2E-H.

claim: The relative abundance of Bacteriodetes and β-Proteobacteria had markedly increased in response to high-phytate diets.
source: Interestingly, the relative abundance of Bacteriodetes and β-Proteobacteria had markedly increased, whereas the relative abundance of Firmicutes had decreased in response to high-phytate diets (Figure 5—figure supplement 2I), suggesting that diets containing high-phytate altered the composition of the gut microbiota.
evidence: The claim is supported by microbiota composition analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2I.

claim: The relative abundance of Firmicutes had decreased in response to high-phytate diets.
source: Interestingly, the relative abundance of Bacteriodetes and β-Proteobacteria had markedly increased, whereas the relative abundance of Firmicutes had decreased in response to high-phytate diets (Figure 5—figure supplement 2I), suggesting that diets containing high-phytate altered the composition of the gut microbiota.
evidence: The claim is supported by microbiota composition analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2I.

claim: Ca2+ supplementation protected rats against the development of severe gross and microscopic changes of renomegaly.
source: Ca2+ supplementation protected these rats against the development of the expected severe gross and microscopic changes of renomegaly (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A–B) and medullary nephrocalcinosis (Figure 5L, Figure 5—figure supplement 3D–F), respectively, as revealed by Alizarin Red S staining.
evidence: The claim is supported by kidney morphology and histology shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3A-B.

claim: Ca2+ supplementation protected rats against medullary nephrocalcinosis.
source: Ca2+ supplementation protected these rats against the development of the expected severe gross and microscopic changes of renomegaly (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A–B) and medullary nephrocalcinosis (Figure 5L, Figure 5—figure supplement 3D–F), respectively, as revealed by Alizarin Red S staining.
evidence: The claim is supported by Alizarin Red S staining shown in Figure 5L and Figure 5—figure supplement 3D-F.

claim: Rats that were fed the HP-HCa2+ diet expressed lower levels of four key markers of renal damage and fibrosis (NGAL, COL1A1, COL6A2, and MPG).
source: Further, rats that were fed the HP-HCa2+ diet expressed lower levels of four key markers (Kronenberg, 2009) of renal damage and fibrosis (NGAL, COL1A1, COL6A2, and MPG) (Figure 5—figure supplement 4A) and exhibited decreased renal fibrosis revealed by Masson's trichrome staining to detect collagen (Figure 5M, Figure 5—figure supplement 4B–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4A.

claim: Rats fed the HP-HCa2+ diet exhibited decreased renal fibrosis.
source: Further, rats that were fed the HP-HCa2+ diet expressed lower levels of four key markers (Kronenberg, 2009) of renal damage and fibrosis (NGAL, COL1A1, COL6A2, and MPG) (Figure 5—figure supplement 4A) and exhibited decreased renal fibrosis revealed by Masson's trichrome staining to detect collagen (Figure 5M, Figure 5—figure supplement 4B–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by Masson's trichrome staining shown in Figure 5M and Figure 5—figure supplement 4B-C.

claim: Rats fed the HP-HCa2+ diet were protected against the expected bone loss and demineralization observed in rats fed the HP-LCa2+ diet.
source: Further, pDEXA and μ-CT analyses of excised femora confirmed that rats fed the HP-HCa2+ diet were protected against the expected bone loss and demineralization observed in rats fed the HP-LCa2+ diet (Figure 5N–O, Figure 5—figure supplement 4D–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by pDEXA and μ-CT analyses shown in Figure 5N-O and Figure 5—figure supplement 4D-G.

claim: Rats fed the HP-LCa2+ diet in conjunction with high PTH had decreased serum levels of 25(OH)D compared with controls.
source: Second, we found that rats fed the HP-LCa2+ diet in conjunction with high PTH had decreased serum levels of 25(OH)D compared with controls (Figure 6B), leading to increased serum levels of 1,25(OH)2D (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by vitamin D measurements shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Rats fed the HP-LCa2+ diet had increased serum levels of 1,25(OH)2D.
source: Second, we found that rats fed the HP-LCa2+ diet in conjunction with high PTH had decreased serum levels of 25(OH)D compared with controls (Figure 6B), leading to increased serum levels of 1,25(OH)2D (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by vitamin D measurements shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The renal expression of αKlotho was significantly decreased in rats fed the HP-LCa2+ diet compared with controls.
source: Immunoblot analysis further confirmed that the renal expression of αKlotho was significantly decreased in rats fed the HP-LCa2+ diet compared with controls (Figure 6G–H Figure 6—figure supplement 1B–C), suggesting that low levels of renal αKlotho may represent a complementary mechanism that increases serum phosphate levels in response to severe hypophosphatemia in rats fed the HP-LCa2+ diet.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 6G-H and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B-C.

claim: Quantitative analysis did not detect significant changes in the serum levels of full-length FGF23 or its C-terminal FGF23 in rats fed the HP-LCa2+ diet compared with controls.
source: Therefore, we analyzed the serum levels of FGF23. Unexpectedly, quantitative analysis did not detect significant changes in the serum levels of full-length FGF23 or its C-terminal FGF23 in rats fed the HP-LCa2+ diet compared with controls (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by ELISA measurements shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D-E.

claim: Rats fed the HP-LCa2+ diet showed decreased levels of FGF23 in the calvarial bones.
source: Immunoblot and immunohistochemical analyses of sections of the femur revealed that rats fed the HP-LCa2+ diet showed decreased levels of FGF23 in the calvarial bones (Figure 6I–J, Figure 6—figure supplement 1F), suggesting that the phytate-mediated renal phosphate wasting was mainly caused by high PTH levels independent of FGF23.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblot and immunohistochemical analyses shown in Figure 6I-J and Figure 6—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Phytate forms insoluble tricalcium- or tetracalcium-phytate salts in vitro over a wide pH range.
source: We previously reported that phytate forms insoluble tricalcium- or tetracalcium-phytate salts in vitro over a wide pH range (Kim et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior research by the authors (Kim et al., 2010).

claim: High-phytate diets cause stronger adverse effects on Ca2+, Fe2+, and Zn2+ levels in infants, young children, and pregnant and lactating women when cereal-based foods represent a large percentage of the diet.
source: High-phytate diets cause stronger adverse effects on Ca2+, Fe2+, and Zn2+ levels in infants, young children, and pregnant and lactating women when cereal-based foods represent a large percentage of the diet (Al Hasan et al., 2016; Chan et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Al Hasan et al., 2016; Chan et al., 2007).

claim: Increasing the levels of phytate reduces the intestinal absorption of Ca2+ and causes nutritional rickets in dogs.
source: Prior studies of dogs demonstrate that increasing the levels of phytate reduces the intestinal absorption of Ca2+ and causes nutritional rickets (Harrison and Mellanby, 1939; Mellanby, 1949).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Harrison and Mellanby, 1939; Mellanby, 1949).

claim: Increasing dietary phytate is associated with secondary hyperparathyroidism in young adults because of the reduced intestinal absorption of dietary Ca2+.
source: Likewise, increasing dietary phytate is associated with secondary hyperparathyroidism in young adults because of the reduced intestinal absorption of dietary Ca2+ (Calvo et al., 1988; Pettifor, 1994).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Calvo et al., 1988; Pettifor, 1994).

claim: Nutritional rickets is more prevalent in children who consume diets comprising low dietary Ca2+ and high phytate.
source: Consistent with previous observations (Ford et al., 1972; Goswami et al., 2000), a subsequent case-control study found that nutritional rickets is more prevalent in children who consume diets comprising low dietary Ca2+ and high phytate (Aggarwal et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Ford et al., 1972; Goswami et al., 2000; Aggarwal et al., 2012).

claim: High-phytate diets inhibit the absorption of glucose and lipids, leading to lower serum levels of glucose, triglycerides, and total cholesterol in humans.
source: For example, high-phytate diets inhibit the absorption of glucose and lipids, leading to lower serum levels of glucose, triglycerides, and total cholesterol in humans (Thompson et al., 1987) and rodents (Kim et al., 2010; Jariwalla et al., 1990; Onomi et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Thompson et al., 1987; Kim et al., 2010; Jariwalla et al., 1990; Onomi et al., 2004).

claim: Diets based on vegetable protein lead to lower plasma levels of phosphate and fibroblast growth factor 23 (FGF23) compared with those based on meat protein.
source: Moreover, diets based on vegetable protein lead to lower plasma levels of phosphate and fibroblast growth factor 23 (FGF23), a major regulator of phosphate homeostasis (Razzaque, 2009), compared with those based on meat protein (Moe et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Razzaque, 2009; Moe et al., 2011).

claim: RANKL is a key component of osteoclastogenesis.
source: Serum levels of receptor activator of nuclear factor kappa-B ligand (RANKL), a key component of osteoclastogenesis (Kong et al., 1999), were markedly increased in high-phytate-fed rats compared with controls (Figure 3F).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior research (Kong et al., 1999) and represents established knowledge.

claim: OPG is a RANKL decoy receptor that inhibits osteoclast differentiation and activation.
source: The levels of osteoprotegerin (OPG), a RANKL decoy receptor that inhibits osteoclast differentiation and activation (Lacey et al., 1998), were significantly reduced (Figure 3G), and the sRANKL/OPG ratio was significantly increased in phytate-fed rats (Figure 3H).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior research (Lacey et al., 1998) and represents established knowledge.

claim: The BUN/Cr ratio is a common laboratory value used to diagnose azotemia and acute kidney injury.
source: The BUN/Cr ratio is a common laboratory value used to diagnose azotemia and acute kidney injury (Uchino et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior research (Uchino et al., 2012) and represents established clinical knowledge.

claim: Multiple inositol polyphosphate phosphatase 1 (MINPP1) is a strong candidate as a histidine acid phytase in humans and other monogastric animals as well as in gut microbiota.
source: Although humans and other monogastric animals, such as pigs, chickens, mice, and rats, are known to lack or have low phytase activities capable of hydrolyzing dietary phytate (Iqbal et al., 1994), recent studies and data in biological databases, such as UniProtKB and the Human Protein Atlas, have suggested that multiple inositol polyphosphate phosphatase 1 (MINPP1) is a strong candidate as a histidine acid phytase in humans and other monogastric animals as well as in gut microbiota (Cho et al., 2006; Stentz et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Iqbal et al., 1994; Cho et al., 2006; Stentz et al., 2014) and database information.

claim: Bacteroidetes express and secrete a homolog of a mammalian MINPP1 in the gut.
source: Phylogenic analysis of bacterial MINPP1 (Stentz et al., 2014) suggested that Bacteroidetes express and secrete a homolog of a mammalian MINPP1 in the gut, whereas Firmicutes, a major phylum of the human intestinal microbiota, do not encode a protein homolog of MINPP1 (Supplementary file 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior research (Stentz et al., 2014) and phylogenetic analysis.

claim: Firmicutes do not encode a protein homolog of MINPP1.
source: Phylogenic analysis of bacterial MINPP1 (Stentz et al., 2014) suggested that Bacteroidetes express and secrete a homolog of a mammalian MINPP1 in the gut, whereas Firmicutes, a major phylum of the human intestinal microbiota, do not encode a protein homolog of MINPP1 (Supplementary file 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis and reference to Supplementary file 5.

claim: Growth retardation and metabolic bone disease are common in children and adolescents who have renal disease.
source: Growth retardation and metabolic bone disease are common in children and adolescents who have renal disease (Wesseling-Perry et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior research (Wesseling-Perry et al., 2012) and represents established clinical knowledge.

claim: Phytate-mediated inhibition of intestinal Ca2+ absorption as well as increased phosphate overload promoted the metabolization of 25(OH)D to 1,25(OH)2D.

claim: The HAPs can only hydrolyze Ca2+-free phytate but cannot hydrolyze Ca2+-phytate when the diet contains a high concentration of Ca2+.

This suggests a mechanism to explain why the HAPs can only hydrolyze Ca2+-free phytate but cannot hydrolyze Ca2+-phytate when the diet contains a high concentration of Ca2+, leading to a decrease in the bioaccessibility of Ca2+-phytate and the bioavailability of intestinal phosphates and Ca2+ for absorption into the blood, eventually leading to excretion of undigested Ca2+-phytate in the feces.

claim: β-propeller phytases mainly have negatively charged amino acids in their active sites.
